html:
The age, from about 250 to 710, when a court centred in the Yamato region near modern Nara grew into the first Japanese state. It is named for the kofun, the huge keyhole-shaped burial mounds of its chiefs.

It followed the farming Yayoi culture. There are about 5,000 keyhole tombs, some among the largest graves in the world, ringed by moats and clay figures. Since written records are thin and the later chronicles are often unreliable, much of what we know comes from archaeology.

Japan learned from the mainland in this period, mostly through Korea:

  • Iron, horse gear and new weapons came from the Korean kingdoms, along with craftsmen among the Toraijin.
  • Chinese writing arrived, and Buddhism came from Baekje, traditionally in 552 or 538.
  • In the Asuka period, from 538, Prince Shotoku issued the Seventeen-article constitution and built temples such as Horyu-ji.

In 645 the Taika Reform began to remake the court on the Chinese model, with land and people belonging to the throne. After Baekje fell in 663, its refugees brought more skills. The period ends in 710 with the move to a fixed capital at Nara, the start of Nara and Heian Japan.
